records.summary: An employer-facing workflow would record consultation, decision reasons and contract changes for proposed workforce changes. Employers would use it to document fire-and-rehire or other contract-change processes.
records.how_money: Employers pay; no price or revenue model is specified.
records.customer: Employers, particularly those considering fire-and-rehire or contract changes.
records.market: UK; the relevant rules apply in England and the wider UK as described in the sources.

revenue_claims.claim: DBT estimates about 12,100 businesses a year (<1% of employers) affected; the estimate may be overstated and is not a forecast of software demand.
Tarn.hr lists £15/month or £150/year for AI HR guidance; it does not yet cover contract changes.
ConsultantLM lists solicitor-led stages from £264 to £3,432.
HRVANTA Etsy toolkit listed at $20.98; the price and sales were unverified.
HRDocBox dismissals toolkit listed at £24.99; price was unverified.

records.paid_demand: No evidence of anyone paying for this niche within the last 18 months was found. Listed competitor prices are offers, not verified sales.

rounds.plain: The January 2027 trigger was supported in this check. No hard-rule failure, two recent direct product launches, official workflow platform or five direct incumbents were found.

The need appears rare and policy aims to reduce it; the start date and rules were still unsettled. Free Acas guidance and existing HR services cover adjacent needs, and no recent payment evidence was found.

risks: The cited commencement regulation was misattributed to fire-and-rehire protections; the supplied deep evidence says it commences a different provision.
The GOV.UK timetable and Acas gave conflicting dates, and the revised Code was still under consultation.
DBT estimated 12,136 employers affected annually before reform, but said the estimate may be overstated; ONS found the practice too rare to publish.
The product cannot guarantee a lawful dismissal; legal content would need human review.
Owner hours are unverified and may exceed 5 h/week while rules are changing.
records.moat: No established moat is described. The rules are public, while free guidance and existing HR services already cover related work.

hours.note: The source says monitoring legal changes and legal review would likely push time above 5 h/week.

records.next_steps: The source does not recommend testing now. If revisited after the Code is finalised (2027), it suggests a one-day landing page offering a contract-change consultation record at £15/month with a refundable reservation, shared through opt-in HR-adviser channels; stop if there are zero reservations from employing companies.

records.summary: A self-serve evidence vault would help in-scope premises and event operators record risk assessments, training and preparedness actions for Martyn’s Law. Operators would pay for the service, though willingness to pay is unverified.
records.how_money: Operators pay; specific paid-plan pricing for this idea is not established.
records.customer: In-scope premises and event operators, with the source recommending focus on enhanced-tier and multi-site operators.
records.market: UK; Martyn’s Law commencement is expected in spring 2027, with no exact date confirmed.

revenue_claims.claim: The Home Office impact assessment estimated 154,623 standard-tier and 24,268 enhanced-tier premises, 178,891 in total; sensitivity range 141,693–208,142. This is an approximate market ceiling, not a count of likely buyers.
Venue Defence lists a free plan, £19.99 per venue/month and £99/month for five venues; paid plans are marked “Coming soon”.
Vigil lists £79/month Standard, £199/month Enhanced and £399/month for up to 10 venues; advertised prices, not verified transactions.
Adjacent training is advertised at £92 + VAT per learner.
No dated, publicly verifiable customer payment or recognised revenue event was found for reviewed evidence-vault competitors.

records.paid_demand: No publicly verifiable customer payments or revenue events were found for the reviewed evidence-vault competitors. Advertised prices, waitlists and free betas do not establish sales.

rounds.plain: Two adjacent readiness products launched within six months: Carlisle’s Scorecard and Accredit Induct. K2 means two or more competing launches in six months.

risks: The estimated premises count is modelled from 2022 data and is not a likely-buyer count.
The SIA is building a notification portal and scope tool and developing templates; standard-tier sites do not submit procedures to the regulator.
Free official guidance and templates may reduce willingness to pay.
No public revenue proof was found for reviewed competitors.
The source does not establish that the product can stay within 5 h/week; security and privacy needs add work.
records.moat: Weak initially: rules are public and competitors already advertise evidence packs, audit trails, staff records and multi-site dashboards. A source-versioned rules engine and venue-specific records could create some switching costs, but the sources do not establish this.

hours.value: Unverified; no evidence it stays at or below 5 h/week
hours.note: The source says a self-serve pilot is needed to measure support, sales and regulatory-update work.

records.next_steps: Run a one-day no-code test: publish a one-page offer for an enhanced-tier or multi-site evidence workspace with a sample pack and opt-in request for a paid pilot or refundable reservation. Use a permitted public industry channel or an agreeing partner; count a qualified paid commitment as the signal to continue.

records.summary: A project checker would map higher-risk building work to the Future Homes and Buildings Standards transition rules and submission milestones. Developers and consultants would pay, but demand and payment evidence are unverified.
records.how_money: Developers and consultants pay; the sources do not specify a price or revenue model.
records.customer: Developers and consultants working on higher-risk building projects.
records.market: England. The cited transition for HRB work commences on 24 September 2027.

revenue_claims.claim: BSR data for July–September 2026 recorded 114 new HRB/conversion Gateway 2 applications and 186 in progress, covering 40,644 units in progress; these are regulated-work counts, not eligible customers.
BSR data recorded 466 HRB internal-work applications received and 1,109 in progress.
Part L Consultant lists developer work from £120 per plot and non-domestic work from £350; a 2026 readiness review is quoted.
FireStrategy.ai lists its broader engineering workspace at £299 per seat monthly or £249 monthly equivalent on annual billing.

records.paid_demand: No independently verifiable payment or revenue evidence was found. A free transition checker already exists, and published service fees are asking prices rather than proof of sales.

competitors.note: Official application-management service, not an identified transition checker.

rounds.plain: The 24 September 2027 transition was supported, and no two recent direct checker launches, official transition-checking platform or five direct incumbents were found.
The rule is real but narrow and time-bound. A free checker already exists, while paid demand and differentiation are unverified.

risks: The transition rules are public and a date calculator alone has little defensibility.
A free Part L transition checker may already cover the core need; its exact HRB outputs are unverified.
The trigger is narrow and time-bound, and high-stakes regulatory answers require careful sourcing and human review.
Owner hours and automation share are unverified; the source says the ≤5 h/week constraint is not demonstrated.
records.moat: A date calculator has little defensibility. A versioned rules engine with clause-level citations, tested edge cases, a change log and per-building decision records could create modest switching costs, but retention and proprietary case data are unverified.

hours.value: ≤5 hours/week is a target, not an evidenced operating figure
hours.note: Depends on self-serve onboarding, limited support and human review of regulatory updates.

records.next_steps: Compare the free Part L checker against published rules using valid pre-deadline, post-deadline, rejected or lapsed, staged and earlier-transition cases. Record missing outputs or citations, make a one-page mock offering a paid pilot, and proceed only if a qualified team shows willingness to pay.

records.summary: A document parser would turn service-charge demands and supporting statements into searchable, comparable records for leaseholders. The idea is for leaseholders to pay, but paid demand is unverified.
records.how_money: Leaseholders would pay; the sources list possible paid checks, reports and reviews but do not establish this product’s pricing.
records.customer: Leaseholders, especially those reviewing service-charge demands and supporting documents.
records.market: England; the source gives a potential population of 4.90 million leasehold dwellings in 2024–25, not likely buyers.

revenue_claims.claim: England had an estimated 4.90 million leasehold dwellings in 2024–25, including 3.38 million flats; potential population, not likely buyers.
Leaseholder owner-occupiers reported a median annual service charge of £1,700.
About 460,000 leaseholders considered making a complaint to their freeholder or management company; complaints covered various topics, with repairs most common.
LEASE reported 1.5 million website visitors and 1.6 million pieces of advice in 2024; service charges were its most common advice topic.
ServiceChargeCheck lists £19.99 for a one-year check and £49.99 with letters; the product is in development.
ServiceCharges.AI lists a £199 Challenge Pack and £49 Buyer Report; the Challenge Pack and £79/month block plan are marked coming soon.
VeraHold lists £49 for a service-charge review and £199 for major works; LeaseScan lists £295 for a one-year audit and £495 for three years; The Lease Translator lists £495 for a lease report.
No verified sales, revenue, or paying-customer count was found for reviewed document-analysis products.

records.paid_demand: No verified sales, revenue or paying-customer counts were found for the reviewed document-analysis products. Competitor prices and free access establish offers, not sales.

rounds.plain: The reforms are planned from 2027, but the check found only one evidenced competing launch within six months and no other evidenced kill rule.
The score record says K2: ServiceCharges.AI and The Lease Translator announced competing service-charge analysis tools within the recent period. K2 means two or more competing launches in six months.

risks: Free AI analysis and benchmarking constrain willingness to pay; no verified sales evidence was found.
The 2027 reform timing is not precise, and standard forms may make basic extraction easier to copy.
Uploading lease and account documents creates data-security and privacy work.
No evidence establishes the automation share or that the product can stay within 5 h/week.
The sources advise keeping the product informational rather than presenting it as legal advice.
records.moat: A permissioned, privacy-protective corpus of multi-year demands, accounts and supporting evidence could become an asset, but this is not established. TPI already publishes a benchmark, and the sources do not show that leaseholders will contribute reusable records or that switching costs would result.

hours.note: No operator time logs or support-volume evidence found.

records.next_steps: Within one day, create a sample searchable comparison from a leaseholder’s voluntarily supplied, redacted demand and accounts. Offer a paid pilot at £19.99 through a moderator-approved public community post, and count only an actual paid pilot with documents supplied as evidence of willingness to pay.
